newsitem.title: PERU: Peru gov't, rebels set for more crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru gov't, rebels set for more crisis talks.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 72 men captive at the Japanese ambassador's home were apparently set on Monday to resume face-to-face talks aimed at a peaceful end to Peru's 83-day hostage crisis.

Rebels and members of a three-man mediating commission set the stage at a 2 1/2-hour meeting on Sunday for negotiations to restart between the government and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA). No starting time was given for the talks, which would be the first since the rebels abruptly called off direct negotiations last week.

Two panel members who met on Sunday with rebel chief Nestor Cerpa told reporters they hoped the week would bring the crisis closer to a peaceful end. "Our message today is that the discussions will continue tomorrow. In the next week, the discussions should be important ones," said Canada's envoy to Peru Anthony Vincent, a mediator.

"We ask everyone involved to let these conversations continue in the way they have, seeking a solution that, although difficult, is viable," added Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, another member of the guarantors commission.

Although the statements did not specifically say the discussions were formal talks between the MRTA and government, state news agency Andina and all local media reported that those negotiations would restart on Monday.

Nine rounds of talks between the MRTA and the government had brought some progress toward a bloodless end to the crisis, with the two sides swapping formal proposals for the first time last week. But a day later the MRTA suspended a 10th meeting, alleging security forces planned to attack the residence through a tunnel.

President Alberto Fujimori has dodged questions about the tunnel while other officials, including Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza, have denied its existence. But some security force sources confirmed four tunnels were dug in recent weeks and local papers gave details, including maps of the tunnels.

Rebels stormed the residence on Dec. 17 and took hundreds of VIPs hostage. Most were released in the first weeks of the siege but the MRTA has kept its most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian envoys and dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats.

Monday began with police at dawn playing music through loudspeakers outside the residence. It was a contrast from Sunday when hundreds of Fujimori supporters staged a noisy rally and hostage sympathisers drove down a nearby street tooting their horns in unison as street hawkers sold crisis T-shirts.

The MRTA, a Cuban-style group believed almost wiped out until it roared back to life in December, is demanding freedom for 458 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages. Fujimori has rejected the demand but suggested he could make other concessions, flying to Cuba last week to arrange asylum for at least some of the rebels as part of a deal to end the crisis.

Fujimori and his allies have refused to rule out using force to free the hostages. "(The government) has to be prepared to act, using all instruments it considers necessary," Congressman Carlos Torres y Torres Lara, a Fujimori ally, said.

The hostages are held on two floors of the building with no electricity, limited water supplies, closed windows and no air conditioning amid one of Lima's hottest summers in memory. Twenty are ill and doctors are occasionally allowed in to treat them.
